The hub's High Likelihood questions for this lecture start with them. Spermatogonia sit in the basal compartment, below the Sertoli cells' tight junctions; primary spermatocytes and spermatids develop in the adluminal compartment, behind the blood-testis barrier. Near their bases, in the basolateral region, neighboring Sertoli cells reach out and touch, joined by occluding, or tight, junctions that form a junctional complex. (Once in class he called them gap junctions; his slide and the rest of the lecture say occluding junctions, and that is the answer.) These junctions divide the tubule into two compartments: a basal compartment next to the basement membrane, and an adluminal compartment, "adluminal" meaning near the lumen. "You need to know the difference between those two," he said. The tight junctions are the blood-testis barrier, and its purpose is to protect the developing gametes from the immune system, which would otherwise attack these rapidly dividing cells. The spermatogonia sit in the basal compartment. Once a type B spermatogonium becomes a primary spermatocyte, it moves straight into the adluminal compartment, behind the barrier, so the spermatocytes and spermatids develop where the immune system cannot reach them. 3 Sertoli cells: shape, the blood-testis barrier and its two compartments, and their jobs (support and nourishment, ABP, AMH, inhibin, phagocytosis, no division, resistant to heat and radiation) Focus list + recording · 5 questions in the bank Know this Sertoli cells support and feed the germ cells, phagocytose shed cytoplasm, make ABP, inhibin and anti-Müllerian hormone, and form the blood-testis barrier. So, from outside in: Leydig cells between the tubules, myoid cells in the wall, Sertoli cells and germ cells in the epithelium. 7 Spermiogenesis: its phases, the nucleus becoming the head, Golgi to acrosome, mitochondria to the middle piece; then spermiation Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank The nucleus elongates, condenses and is reshaped into the main bulk of the sperm head. The mitochondria gather in the middle piece, where their ATP powers the tail. He lists three to four phases, depending on whether the cap and acrosomal phases are counted separately: the Golgi phase, the cap or acrosomal phase, and the maturation phase. The process ends with spermiation, the release of the sperm from the Sertoli cell. The excess cytoplasm stays behind, and his best guess is that the Sertoli cell phagocytoses it, which fits its job of phagocytosing the cytoplasm shed during sperm development. 8 The spermatic cord: the ductus deferens with the testicular artery and the pampiniform plexus (the only two other parts he said to know) Flagged in the recording · 1 question in the bank Know this Spermatic cord: the ductus deferens plus the testicular artery and the pampiniform plexus of veins. The vas is only one part of the spermatic cord; the cord also carries the vessels and nerves. Of its other parts, "the only two components that I really think you should know about" are the testicular artery, which supplies the testis with blood, and the pampiniform plexus of veins. Pampiniform means formed like the tendrils of a vine that reach out and wrap around whatever it grows on. The spermatic cord is where the vas is cut in a vasectomy. 9 Accessory glands: seminal vesicles (70 percent, fructose, lipochrome), the prostate around the urethra (trouble urinating, PSA, alkaline first portion), bulbourethral glands (lubrication, skeletal muscle under somatic control) Flagged in the recording · 7 questions in the bank Structure Coiled tubular glands, about 15 cm 30 to 50 compound tubuloalveolar glands in three sets, wrapped around the urethra Small, bulb-shaped mucous glands Lining and wall Pseudostratified columnar; smooth muscle, inner circular and outer longitudinal Simple or pseudostratified columnar; fibromuscular stroma Skeletal muscle between the units (somatic control) Key products Fructose, prostaglandins, proteins Citric acid, acid phosphatase, fibrinolysin, PSA, amylase, prostaglandins Galactose and sialic acid When and how much About 70 percent of the volume The first portion of the ejaculate Before the emission of semen Slide clue Yellow lipochrome pigment Concretions (corpora amylacea) Skeletal muscle 10 The penis: two corpora cavernosa fill, the corpus spongiosum keeps the urethra open; erection by relaxed smooth muscle; point and shoot Flagged in the recording · 3 questions in the bank Know this The two corpora cavernosa fill with blood; the corpus spongiosum around the urethra fills much less, so the urethra stays open. The urethra runs instead in the corpus spongiosum, which is softer and fills with far less blood. That keeps the urethra open, so semen can pass during erection. "If we had a corpus cavernosum around the urethra, there wouldn't be many human beings." Erection results from relaxation of the trabecular and arterial smooth muscle: the central arteries dilate and the cavernous spaces of the two corpora cavernosa fill with blood. His summary slide adds the third step, compression of the venous outflow against the tunica albuginea: the swelling tissue presses the draining veins against the unyielding tunica, so blood that has come in cannot get out, and the tissue stays rigid. Relax, fill, trap. The common mistake is to think the smooth muscle contracts. It relaxes. His slide's flaccid-and-erect blood supply figure (helicine arteries from the deep artery filling the cavernous spaces, nutritive arteries to the trabeculae, arteriovenous shunts, the deep veins) is one he said "you don't need to know ... necessarily." 11 The epididymis: its lining, its three jobs, sperm maturation and glycerophosphocholine against capacitation Flagged in the recording · 4 questions in the bank Maturation, over 2 to 12 days: the sperm's chromatin is stabilized, its plasma membrane changes (his slide: its surface charge), it acquires new surface proteins, and it becomes motile, gaining forward motility. Transport of sperm toward the ductus deferens, by peristalsis to the storage region in the tail. 12 The ducts in order and their linings: tubuli recti, rete testis, efferent ductules (cilia) vs ductus deferens, epididymis and vas (stereocilia) Flagged in the recording · 2 questions in the bank His overview slide shortens this and calls the straight ducts the rete testis; his duct slide separates them. Learn the longer version: tubuli recti first, then the rete testis. Watch the two look-alike names too. In his overview he once said the rete testis connects to the "ductus deferens," which leads into the epididymis; he meant the ductus efferentes, and he gives the right order later in the lecture. The efferent ductules come before the epididymis; the ductus deferens comes after it. Also flagged in class Keep the two chains apart: LH, Leydig, testosterone; FSH, Sertoli, androgen-binding protein. About 74 days in the tubules, then 2 to 12 days of maturation in the epididymis (Dr. Madison's physiology lecture says about two months). Seminal vesicles: about 70 percent of the volume, fructose for energy, and the lipochrome pigment that fluoresces under UV light. An enlarged prostate compresses the urethra it wraps around; expect a patient who has trouble urinating. Bulbourethral glands: skeletal muscle between the units, so somatic (voluntary) control; their galactose and sialic acid mucus lubricates before the emission of semen. Erection is parasympathetic; ejaculation is sympathetic. You can skip Don't memorize how micrographs look; know the drawings and what each structure is, where it sits and what it does.
